docs.title: Parakeet
docs.text:
A data-parallel compiler for numerical Python.

Write the calculation with NumPy or compose maps, folds and scans directly. Parakeet specializes the function for its inputs and fuses array operations before generating native code for CPUs, Apple Metal or NVIDIA CUDA.

Get started Explore the gallery

docs.title: Exact nearest neighbor
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from parakeet import jit


@jit
def nearest(x, y):
  delta = x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]
  d2 = np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2)
  return np.argmin(d2, axis=1)

On CPU, Parakeet computes distances a tile at a time and keeps the winning reference index for each query. Ties return the first index.

Compare timings and allocations

docs.title: Inside the compiler
docs.text:
• Fusion. Two histogram expressions with the same bin IDs can accumulate gradient and Hessian together in one traversal. See the tree-split example.
  • Tiling. A normalized weighted sum can consume its scores in blocks. Gaussian regression and attention share that reduction. See the algebraic laws.
  • Differentiation. Differentiate a scalar loss over arrays with grad or value_and_grad. See the differentiation guide.
  • Inspection. Examine the operator IR, the rewrites that fired and the generated code. Inspect a rewrite.

Parakeet began as a research compiler at New York University. The 1.0 rewrite retains its algebra of array operators and extends it to modern Python and GPUs. History, papers and language boundaries.

docs.title: Algebraic laws & frontier kernels
docs.text:
Modern high-performance kernels — FlashAttention-2/3, FlashDecoding, FlexAttention, Apple Cut Cross-Entropy (CCE), DeepSeek Multi-Head Latent Attention (FlashMLA), Llama-3 Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and Mamba-2 State-Space Duality (SSD) — rarely get their order-of-magnitude speedups from writing tighter scalar loops. They get them by eliminating $O(N^2)$, $O(N \cdot V)$, or $O(T)$ memory round-trips and sequential bottlenecks using a small set of universal algebraic laws.

Parakeet encodes these laws directly as general IR passes over its five data-parallel operators (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexScatter, IndexTile) plus multi-state Carry folds and TileStage SRAM staging. None of these passes hard-code "Transformer" or "LLM" layers: the exact same rewrite rules fire on RBF/Gaussian kernel regression, tropical shortest-path algorithms, exact nearest-neighbor search, GBDT histogram split-finding, and Kalman/IIR filters.

docs.title: Law 1 — Rescaled semiring monoids
docs.text:
Any reduction whose output depends on a global normalizing statistic (a maximum $m$, sum of exponentials $l$, mean $\mu$, or norm) can be fused with downstream contractions in a single SRAM-tiled pass whenever its state forms an associative monoid $(S, \oplus, e)$.

For softmax-weighted contractions (FlashAttention, FlashDecoding, RBF kernel regression), the monoid carries running row maximum $m$, denominator $l$, and unnormalized output vector $\mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^D$:

$$ (m_1, l_1, \mathbf{o}_1) \oplus (m_2, l_2, \mathbf{o}_2) = \Big(m,\; l_1 e^{m_1 - m} + l_2 e^{m_2 - m},\; \mathbf{o}_1 e^{m_1 - m} + \mathbf{o}_2 e^{m_2 - m}\Big), \quad m = \max(m_1, m_2) $$

Because $\oplus$ is strictly associative, the exact same monoid simultaneously produces:

  1. FlashAttention (kind="flash_monoid"): streams tiles of $K_j, V_j$ through GPU __shared__ / threadgroup memory against hoisted $Q_i$ without ever allocating the $O(N^2)$ score matrix $S$ or probability matrix $P$.
  2. FlashDecoding (split_k=True): when the query grid is small relative to device SMs (e.g. autoregressive decode $T_q \le 16$, $T_{kv} \ge 128$), Parakeet splits $T_{kv}$ across parallel threadblocks computing partial $(m_p, l_p, \mathbf{o}_p)$ and recombines them using the exact same $\oplus$.
  3. Cut Cross-Entropy (kind="monoid_lse"): tiles $H W^\top$ over vocabulary $V$ with the scalar $(m, l)$ monoid plus on-the-fly target dot-product gather, never materializing the $O(M \cdot V)$ logit matrix.
  4. RBF / Gaussian Kernel Regression (score_op="sqdist"): recognizes $-\gamma |x_i - y_j|_2^2$ as a tiled contraction feeding softmax and compiles Nadaraya-Watson smoothing into a single $O(N + M)$-memory kernel.

docs.title: Law 2 — Algebraic rematerialization in reverse-mode AD
docs.text:
Standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation saves every forward intermediate on the tape, which immediately re-introduces $O(N^2)$ memory for attention and $O(M \cdot V)$ memory for cross-entropy. Parakeet's tape optimizer (parakeet/transforms/algebraic_vjp.py) runs at the high-level operator level before lowering and rewrites known structures into sufficient-statistic algebraic VJPs:

  • Attention backward (flash_monoid_bwd): saves only $(Q, K, V, O, \text{lse})$ — zero $N \times N$ tensors saved. A cheap $O(ND)$ pre-pass computes $D_i = \sum_d dO_{id} O_{id}$, and the SRAM-tiled backward kernel recomputes each tile $P_{ij} = \exp(S_{ij} - \text{lse}i)$ and $dS(dO_i V_j^\top - D_i)$ on-chip while accumulating $dK, dV$ in registers.} = P_{ij
  • Cut Cross-Entropy backward (cce_bwd): saves only $(H, W, y, \text{lse})$ — zero $M \times V$ logits saved. A 2D-tiled GPU kernel recomputes $p_{iv} = \exp(h_i \cdot w_v - \text{lse}_i)$ in SRAM and accumulates $dH, dW$.
  • LayerNorm & RMSNorm VJP: collapses multi-pass mean/variance/sqrt backward graphs into a single algebraic VJP over saved $(\hat{x}, \sigma)$, eliminating redundant reductions.
  • Standalone Softmax VJP: eliminates the max backward entirely via $dS = P \odot (dP - \sum P \odot dP)$.

docs.title: Law 3 — Bilinear contraction reassociation & shared-KV tiling
docs.text:
For any chain of two bilinear contractions sharing a single-use intermediate $T$:

$$ T[u, k] = \sum_{r=0}^{R-1} U[u, r]\, V[k, r], \qquad Y[p, u] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} W[p, k]\, T[u, k] $$

reassociating the contraction order yields the identical tensor:

$$ M[p, r] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} W[p, k]\, V[k, r], \qquad Y[p, u] = \sum_{r=0}^{R-1} M[p, r]\, U[u, r] $$

parakeet/transforms/reassociate.py compares the exact multiply-add counts $U K (R + P)$ vs $P R (K + U)$:

  • DeepSeek MLA weight absorption: Given naive K = C_kv @ W_uk; V = C_kv @ W_uv; O = softmax(Q @ K.T) @ V, Law 3 emits a cost-guarded branch that absorbs $W_{uk}$ into $Q$ (Q_abs = Q @ W_uk.T) and moves $W_{uv}$ after attention (O_lat = P @ C_kv; O = O_lat @ W_uv). Because monoidal tiling (Law 1) runs immediately after Law 3 and recurses into both branches, the decode branch automatically fuses into FlashMLA / FlashDecoding directly over the compressed latent C_kv — never decompressing K or V into HBM. When $T_q$ is large (prefill), the runtime guard picks the lower-FLOP decompressed branch automatically.
  • General low-rank chains (LoRA, Kronecker): (X @ A) @ B and X @ (A @ B) automatically select the FLOP-optimal order at runtime with full reverse-mode AD support.
  • GQA head-group tiling: When a trailing batch axis g of Q (extent G) does not appear in K or V (e.g. Q: (B, H_kv, G, T_q, D), K, V: (B, H_kv, 1, T_kv, D)), Parakeet folds g into the query row tile (i_eff = g * T_q + i), serving all G query heads from a single SRAM load of K and V.

docs.title: Law 4 — Chunkwise state-space duality (TileScan)
docs.text:
Sequential recurrences over length $T$ have $O(T)$ serial depth and cannot saturate multi-core CPUs or GPUs directly. parakeet/transforms/tile_scan.py recognizes two general associative recurrence structures inside plain Python for t in range(T): loops:

  1. Affine linear recurrences ($s_t = a_t s_{t-1} + b_t$ — EMA, IIR filters, scalar Kalman filters, RG-LRU, GBDT histogram prefix sums): Rewrites the loop into a 3-stage parallel chunkwise scan (C = 64) using the associative affine composition monoid $(a_2, b_2) \circ (a_1, b_1) = (a_2 a_1,\; a_2 b_1 + b_2)$ — cutting sequential depth by $64\times$ with zero $O(T)$ temporary arrays.
  2. Bilinear matrix-state recurrences (Mamba-2 SSD & Gated Linear Attention): 
    for t in range(T):
  S = a[t] * S + k[t][:, None] * v[t][None, :]
  out[t] = q[t] @ S
    Rewrites the 6-line sequential loop into 4-step division-free Chunkwise State-Space Duality (C = 64):
  3. Step 0: parallel division-free cumulative decay products (exact even when $a_t = 0$ or $a_t < 0$, and for $T$ not divisible by $C$).
  4. Step 1: intra-chunk quadratic attention-form GEMMs $M^{(c)} = (Q^{(c)} {K^{(c)}}^\top) \odot L^{(c)}$, $Y_{\text{intra}}^{(c)} = M^{(c)} V^{(c)}$.
  5. Step 2: chunk state summary GEMM $B^{(c)} = (\tilde{K}^{(c)})^\top V^{(c)}$.
  6. Step 3: $64\times$-shorter inter-chunk recurrence $S_{\text{in}}^{(c+1)} = A^{(c)} S_{\text{in}}^{(c)} + B^{(c)}$.
  7. Step 4: off-diagonal readout GEMM $Y_{\text{off}}^{(c)} = Q^{(c)} S_{\text{in}}^{(c)}$ and parallel combine.

Because chunkwise scan runs right before tiling, all four heavy steps compile automatically to NVIDIA CUDA nvcuda::wmma Tensor Cores, Apple Metal simdgroup_matrix, and CPU register micro-tiles.

docs.title: Law 5 — Affine tile-interval mask pruning
docs.text:
In parakeet/transforms/analysis.py, TileInterval propagates bounding intervals $[i_0, i_0 + B_M - 1]$ and $[j_0, j_0 + B_N - 1]$ through arbitrary affine index expressions and boolean connectives:

  • Causal mask (j <= i): proves j0 > i0 + BM - 1 is all-false (entire upper-triangular block skipped before loading K or V!) and j0 + BN - 1 <= i0 is all-true (branchless inner loop!).
  • Sliding-window / FlexAttention ((j <= i) & (i - j <= W)): automatically skips both future tiles and past tiles outside window W — turning $O(N^2)$ attention into $O(N \cdot W)$ without writing a custom sparse kernel.
  • Runtime boolean masks: when a mask comes from a runtime boolean array, the GPU kernel performs a cooperative SRAM ballot across the tile and skips all-false tiles before any dot-product or value loads.

docs.title: Inspecting rewrites with parakeet.dsl
docs.text:
Use parakeet.dsl.show_rewrite on any function to see which algebraic laws fired, which MonoidalTilePlans were synthesized, and the before/after IR:

import numpy as np
import parakeet
from parakeet import dsl


@parakeet.jit
def causal_attention(q, k, v):
  causal = dsl.imap(lambda ij: ij[0] >= ij[1], (q.shape[0], k.shape[0]))
  s = np.where(causal, (q @ k.T) * np.float32(0.125), np.float32(-1e9))
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ v


q = np.zeros((128, 64), np.float32)
print(dsl.show_rewrite(causal_attention, q, q, q).summary())

Parakeet Algebraic Rewrite Report for `causal_attention`
  Laws triggered : Law 1: Rescaled Semiring Monoid Tile Fusion, Law 5: Affine Tile-Interval Mask Pruning
  Monoidal plans : flash_monoid
  Operators      : IndexMap 5 -> 1 | IndexTile 1 | IndexScatter 0 | Carry folds 0

See the Gallery of examples for runnable benchmarks across all six laws.

docs.title: parakeet.jit
docs.text:
Compile a numerical Python function to native code on first call.

Use it bare (@jit) or with options (@jit(backend="metal")). The function is specialised for each distinct combination of argument types; every later call with the same types runs the cached native code.

Options (all default to the corresponding parakeet.config setting):

backend "auto", "c", "multicore", "threads", "openmp", "gcd", "metal"/"mps", "cuda" or "python". bounds_check Raise IndexError for out-of-range indices instead of crashing. fusion Fuse array expressions into single loops. tiling Tile matmul-shaped loops for cache locality.

docs.title: Gradients
docs.text:
grad turns a function into its gradient. It is an adverb like map and reduce: it is applied while your code is compiled, and what comes out is ordinary loops that are fused, tiled and run in parallel like everything else.

import numpy as np
from parakeet import grad, value_and_grad


def loss(w, x, y):
  return np.mean((np.tanh(x @ w) - y) ** 2)


g = grad(loss)(w, x, y)  # d loss / d w, shaped like w
value, g = value_and_grad(loss)(w, x, y)
gw, gx = grad(loss, (0, 1))(w, x, y)  # several arguments at once

The function has to return one floating point number. The arguments you differentiate with respect to can be floats, float arrays, or tuples of those nested however you like — the gradient comes back with the same structure:

def mlp(params, x, y):
  (w1, b1), (w2, b2) = params
  h = np.tanh(x @ w1 + b1)
  return np.mean((h @ w2 + b2 - y) ** 2)


(gw1, gb1), (gw2, gb2) = grad(mlp)(params, x, y)

grad(f) can be called from plain Python, where it compiles on first use, or inside a @jit function, where the whole training step becomes one compiled function:

@jit
def descend(w, x, y, rate, steps):
  for _ in range(steps):
    w = w - rate * grad(loss)(w, x, y)
  return w

examples/nanogpt.py trains a small transformer this way, and examples/convnet.py a convolutional network.

docs.title: What can be differentiated
docs.text:
arithmetic and math functions + - * / **, np.exp, np.tanh, np.maximum, np.where, np.abs, np.clip, … with broadcasting reductions np.sum, np.mean, np.var, np.std, np.max, np.min, np.prod, np.linalg.norm, with axis and keepdims; parakeet.reduce with add, multiply, minimum, maximum linear algebra @, np.dot, np.matmul for vectors, matrices and stacks of matrices; np.einsum running and ordered np.cumsum, parakeet.scan(add, x), np.sort folds parakeet.reduce(f, x) with any function f views slicing, x.T, reshape, ravel, np.transpose, x[:, None] indexing with arrays x[idx], x[rows, cols] building arrays np.concatenate, np.stack, np.array([a, b, c]), comprehensions adverbs map/each, allpairs, imap with your own functions, including functions that use arrays from outside scalar code anything written with scalars, conditional expressions included

Derivatives of min, max, abs and friends at a tie follow the usual conventions: ties in a reduction share the gradient equally.

docs.title: Loops and branches
docs.text:
The derivative is laid out when the function is compiled, so the compiler has to know how many times each operation runs.

A for loop over a tuple, or over a range whose length is known when the function is compiled, is unrolled: a literal, a scalar argument, or the shape of an array all work. Such an argument becomes part of what the function is specialized on, exactly like axis=.

def deep(weights, x):  # a tuple of matrices
  for w in weights:
    x = np.tanh(x @ w)
  return np.sum(x)


def correlate(x, kernel):
  out = x[: len(x) - len(kernel) + 1] * 0.0
  for i in range(len(kernel)):  # unrolled: one specialization per kernel length
    out = out + x[i : i + len(out)] * kernel[i]
  return np.sum(out**2)

Loops that do not touch differentiated values are left alone, so a training loop around grad is an ordinary loop.

What cannot be unrolled cannot be differentiated: while loops, loops over the elements of an array of unknown length, and anything longer than 4096 iterations. Use an array operation or an adverb instead — np.sum, parakeet.map, a comprehension.

An if statement whose condition is only known at run time is differentiated by running both branches and choosing between their results, which is what np.where does. That is only possible when running the branch not taken has no effect, so the branches may only assign variables: no return, raise, break, no stores into arrays, no in-place updates. Remember that both sides are computed: if x > 0: y = np.log(x) evaluates the logarithm either way.

if np.sum(x) > 10.0:  # fine
  h, scale = np.tanh(h), 2.0
else:
  h, scale = h * h, 3.0

A guard that only raises (if n == 0: raise ValueError(...)) is fine too, and is not run for both sides.

docs.title: Writing into arrays
docs.text:
Stores are differentiated: assigning a slice, an element, or updating in place all work, in straight-line code and in loops that can be unrolled.

out = np.zeros((n, 3))
out[:3] = x[:3] @ w
out[3:] = np.tanh(x[3:] @ w)
out += bias

Going backwards, whatever adjoint arrived for the stored region belongs to the value that was stored, and the region starts again from zero.

One thing cannot work: overwriting a value that an earlier operation's derivative still has to read. y = np.tanh(h); h[0] = 5.0 is refused, because the derivative of tanh needs the old h; y = np.sum(h * 3.0); h[0] = 5.0 is fine, because that derivative does not. Stores through an array of indices (out[idx] = v) are not differentiated.

docs.title: The gradient is right or there is none
docs.text:
Parakeet never returns a gradient that silently ignores part of your function. If something on the way from the arguments to the result has no derivative rule — np.cumprod, np.convolve, a scan with your own function — you get an UnsupportedError naming it:

UnsupportedError: cannot differentiate through cumprod() (line 12): its derivative is not implemented

docs.title: Second derivatives
docs.text:
grad of a function that calls grad works for element-wise operators, reductions, matrix products and views — enough for gradient penalties and Hessian-vector products:

def penalty(w, x):
  g = grad(loss)(w, x)  # the gradient, as part of the function
  return np.sum(g * g)


grad(penalty)(w, x)  # 2 H g, reverse over reverse

It is refused, by name, through map with your own function, indexing with arrays, cumsum, sort, folds and np.stack/np.concatenate.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
A gradient costs about two to three times the function. Element-wise chains are fused in both directions; a matrix product's derivative is two more matrix products.

The derivative of map/allpairs with your own function runs in parallel like the map itself. Every element may add to the gradient of an array the function captured (the weights of a network mapped over a batch), so each chunk of the loop adds to a copy of its own and the copies are summed at the end: a reduction whose accumulator is the whole gradient. That costs memory: one copy of the captured parameters per thread, up to 256 MB, beyond which fewer chunks are used.

Loops are unrolled, so a long unrolled loop makes for a long compile.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
While the function is elaborated, a tape records each array operator applied to a value that depends on the differentiated arguments. The record is made where the operator still has its algebraic meaning, so each rule is one line: an element-wise operator becomes a map of the scalar function's partial derivative, a sum broadcasts its adjoint back, a matrix product becomes two more, a map differentiates its function again per element.

Scalars are not recorded. An expression in Parakeet's IR is already a record of how it was computed, so the adjoint of a scalar is pushed straight down its expression tree. Views are not recorded either: a slice of an array is the same slice of its adjoint.

See parakeet/transforms/autodiff.py.

docs.title: Backends and GPUs
docs.text:
Every backend runs the same compiled host program (C). They differ in how the parallel loops inside it are executed.

backend Parallel loops run on Notes "auto" the best multi-core strategy found default; same as "multicore" "c" the calling thread no threads at all; also compiles without parallel loop overhead "threads" Parakeet's persistent thread pool POSIX; fork-safe; no extra runtime library "gcd" Grand Central Dispatch macOS "openmp" the compiler's OpenMP runtime needs libgomp/libomp (macOS: brew install libomp) "metal" / "mps" the Apple GPU pip install "parakeet[metal]==1.0.0" "cuda" an NVIDIA GPU pip install "parakeet[cuda12]==1.0.0" (CuPy) "python" — runs the original function uncompiled 
parakeet.available_backends()
# {'python': 'ok', 'c': 'ok', 'threads': 'ok', 'gcd': 'ok', 'openmp': 'ok', 'metal': 'ok',
#  'cuda': 'unavailable: the CUDA backend needs CuPy, which is not installed. Install ...'}

A backend that cannot work fails when you select it, with a message saying what is missing and how to install it — not later with a linker error.

docs.title: Multi-core
docs.text:
Array expressions, map/allpairs/imap, comprehensions, parfor and reductions over recognised associative operations are split into chunks that run on parakeet.config.num_threads threads (default: all cores). Only the outermost data-parallel operation is parallelised; anything nested inside it runs sequentially within each thread.

Small loops are not worth a thread hand-off: loops with a cheap body run on the calling thread unless they have at least 2 * config.parallel_grain iterations (default 8192 per chunk). Loops whose body contains loops of its own are always split.

Compiled functions release the GIL and are safe to call from several Python threads at once. With multiprocessing, prefer the spawn start method when using "openmp" or "gcd" (those runtimes do not survive fork); the default thread pool does.

docs.title: Apple GPUs (Metal)
docs.text:
@jit(backend="metal")
def blur_energy(img):
  return (img[1:-1, 1:-1] * 4 - img[:-2, 1:-1] - img[2:, 1:-1] - img[1:-1, :-2] - img[1:-1, 2:]) ** 2

Each eligible parallel loop is also compiled to a Metal compute kernel; the host program hands loops of at least config.device_threshold iterations (default 32768) to the GPU and runs smaller ones on the CPU.

Apple GPUs have no float64

Metal does not support double precision. A loop that touches float64 data runs on the CPU thread pool instead, and Parakeet emits a FallbackWarning saying so. Pass float32 arrays and np.float32 scalars to stay on the GPU (a Python float argument is a double; x * 2.0 with a literal is fine).

Other reasons a loop stays on the CPU: it allocates temporary arrays per iteration, or it uses a function Metal lacks (lgamma, erfc). The warning always names the reason. Control this with config.device_fallback: "warn" (default), "silent", or "error" to refuse instead.

Runtime errors inside kernels (out-of-bounds indices, failed assertions) are reported as normal Python exceptions.

docs.title: NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA)
docs.text:
@jit(backend="cuda")
def distances(X, C):
  return parakeet.allpairs(lambda a, b: np.sum((a - b) ** 2), X, C)

Kernels are compiled at run time by CuPy's RawKernel (NVRTC), so only the NVIDIA driver and a CuPy wheel matching your CUDA version are needed. All dtypes including float64 are supported. The same per-loop fallback rules apply.

Validation status

CI has no NVIDIA hardware, so there the CUDA code generator runs against a simulator (PARAKEET_CUDA_SIMULATE=1) that compiles the generated kernels as C++ and executes their thread grid on the CPU.

The 1.0 release comparison ran on a physical NVIDIA A10 with strict device dispatch. Earlier checks on an A100 (Google Colab, CuPy with CUDA 13, Python 3.13) and Tesla T4 covered the whole test suite with every parallel loop forced onto the GPU (688 tests, including the tiled products, the gradient tests and arrays kept on the device between loops), the examples and the benchmarks all passed. That check is run on demand, not by CI:

pip install runplz google-colab-cli
runplz colab tools/colab_job.py          # T4; PK_COLAB_GPU=A100 for others

To push your own test suite through a GPU set PARAKEET_TEST_BACKENDS=cuda (the backends used by parakeet.testing.expect and check) and PARAKEET_DEVICE_THRESHOLD=1 (so small arrays go to the device too).

docs.title: What about TPUs?
docs.text: No. A TPU only runs programs compiled by XLA, which wants whole-array operations with static shapes; Parakeet generates scalar loops in C-like kernel languages. Parakeet's CPU backends do work on a Colab TPU host (24 x86 cores), which is all PK_COLAB_TPU=v5e1 runplz colab tools/colab_job.py checks.

docs.title: How data moves
docs.text:
Arrays belong to the host, but within one call they stay on the device.

  • The first GPU loop that uses an array puts it on the device. A buffer the host allocated and has not written to yet (the output of the loop, usually) is created there directly: nothing is copied. On Metal, arrays allocated by compiled code are shared with the GPU without copying at all.
  • Later loops find the array already there. What a loop wrote stays on the device; it is not copied back after every loop.
  • Host code that reads or writes array memory itself (an explicit Python loop, a loop that fell back to the CPU, a call into the BLAS) first asks for everything the device has changed. So does the end of the call.
  • A temporary that is freed before anyone on the host looked at it is never copied back.

A chain of array operations on a GPU therefore costs one upload of its inputs and one download of its result, however many loops it has. Mixing GPU loops with scalar host loops over the same arrays works, and gives the same answers, but pays for a download and an upload each time the two alternate.

Which loops go to the device. A loop is sent when its number of elements times the estimated inner iterations per element reaches config.device_threshold, and it has at least 1024 elements. A loop over 5,000 rows that each need a 10,000-step inner loop goes; a loop over 20,000 cheap elements stays on the CPU, where the launch would cost more than the work; so does a loop over 32 features however long each one's scan is, because a device runs one (slow) thread per element and 32 of them are no match for a few CPU cores.

Use parakeet.to_device(x, backend="cuda") or backend="metal" to reuse resident array inputs across calls. Pass the resulting device arrays to a compiled function and call parakeet.to_host(result) when Python needs the data. Operations which run on the host can still require transfers.

docs.title: 1.0.0 (November 24, 2026)
docs.text: A ground-up rewrite for modern Python. The @jit decorator, the adverbs (map, reduce, scan, allpairs, imap, ...) and the overall idea are unchanged; everything underneath is new.

docs.title: Algebraic operators
docs.text:
• The same CPU tile schedule serves exact nearest-neighbor queries written as broadcasting NumPy or nested parallel maps. It merges a distance and index per query and preserves the first index on ties.
  • Two weighted histograms over shared bin IDs can fuse into a single traversal. Structured folds accept tuples and named records with a user-defined merge.
  • Algebraic rewrites cover online normalized sums, their gradients, reassociation of contractions, and chunked affine scans. The rewrite inspector shows which passes fired for a given function and input.
  • The gallery includes runnable examples. The release benchmarks compare five workloads with general-purpose and specialist implementations on a four-vCPU worker and an NVIDIA A10.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• grad and value_and_grad: reverse-mode differentiation as an adverb. Element-wise operators, reductions, matrix products, views, map and allpairs with your own functions all have derivative rules; loops of known length are unrolled; anything without a rule raises instead of returning a wrong gradient. examples/nanogpt.py and examples/convnet.py train with it.
  • More of grad: cumsum, sort, einsum, stacks of matrices, folds with any function, and if statements on run-time conditions (both branches run, results are selected). The derivative of a map runs in parallel.
  • A middle end: elaboration now produces operator statements (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, printed by spec.operators) and a pipeline of passes rewrites them before they become loops. Tiling is one such pass, a pattern match on the IR instead of a trial elaboration; vertical fusion (Map→Map including matmul epilogues, Scan→Map into emit, Map→Filter, Map→Reduce), filter fusion (Filter→Filter and Filter→Reduce: np.sum(x[x > 0]) is one loop and allocates nothing), sibling fusion (x.min(), x.max() and np.sin(x), np.cos(x) each share one loop), reduction interchange (np.sum(X, axis=0) becomes L1-tiled contiguous SIMD loops), and dead-operator elimination all run at this level; find_broken_transform bisects the pass list; config.skip_transforms switches passes off.
  • General operators: reduce, scan and filter take several arrays with map= (and emit=); np.einsum; @ on stacks; reductions over several axes in one pass; tiling for maps of any rank.
  • Parallel primitives: prefix scans (cumsum), filters (x[mask], nonzero) and argmin/argmax run in parallel, on CPUs and GPUs.
  • GPU: arrays stay on the device between the loops of one call; a loop is sent to the device by the work in it, not its element count.
  • BLAS: float matrix products call the BLAS NumPy uses.
  • Tiling: two-dimensional maps of reductions (@, allpairs distances, ...) run a cache-sized tile at a time with their reductions jammed 2×4. A 1024×1024 matrix product is 2× faster on one core and 3× on all of them.
  • np.sort and np.argsort take axis and sort every lane in parallel (N-d input used to be flattened without saying so).
  • The dimensions of an array argument can be compile-time constants when the code needs them to be (range(w.shape[0]) in a loop that must be unrolled).
  • parakeet.macro and parakeet.find_broken_transform are back, and the code is laid out in frontend/, syntax/, transforms/ and lib/ again.
  • Faster compiles for large functions: identical loop bodies are compiled once.
  • Checked on real NVIDIA hardware. The whole suite passes with every parallel loop forced onto a Tesla T4 (tools/colab_job.py, run on demand with runplz colab; not part of CI).
  • Reads like Parakeet again: two-space indentation, parakeet.prims and parakeet.ndtypes, and the 0.x helpers typed_repr, specialize, run_python_fn, openmp_available, rank/size/shape, plus the old config.opt_fusion / config.print_* option names.

  • Fixed: two arguments of one GPU kernel that view the same memory now share a device buffer (previously one of them could read a truncated copy).

  • Python 3.11+ and NumPy 2, no dependencies besides NumPy and a C compiler (the dsltools, appdirs, llvmpy and PyCUDA dependencies are gone).

  • New frontend. Functions are elaborated directly into a typed loop IR: calls are inlined, closures/tuples/slices are resolved at compile time, and array expressions are fused into their consumers.
  • Backends: sequential C; multi-core through a built-in thread pool, OpenMP or Grand Central Dispatch; Apple GPUs through Metal; NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA (CuPy/NVRTC, no nvcc needed). GPU backends fall back to the CPU per loop, with a warning that says why.
  • NumPy-exact typing (NEP 50): result dtypes match NumPy, including the treatment of Python scalars.
  • Safety: bounds checks, shape checks, division and domain checks raise the same exceptions NumPy/Python would; compile errors carry the source location and the chain of inlined calls; reference-counted temporaries are freed eagerly (no more leaks in loops).
  • Much larger language subset: early return, break/continue, while, keyword/default/*args arguments, walrus, assert/raise, boolean-mask and integer-array indexing (reads and writes), in-place operators with NumPy aliasing semantics, 0-d and empty arrays, all integer/float dtypes.
  • Much larger library: ~200 NumPy functions and methods, np.random (a counter-based generator that is reproducible in parallel and on GPUs), sorting, math, and most numeric builtins.
  • Globals and closure variables are read at call time (no stale constants); arguments that must be compile-time constants (such as axis) are specialised on demand.
  • Compiled modules are cached on disk and shared between processes.
  • parakeet.config, parakeet.options(...), PARAKEET_* environment variables, f.specialize(...).ir/.source/.kernels, available_backends().

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings live on parakeet.config. Assign to change them for the process, use parakeet.options(...) to change them temporarily, pass backend, bounds_check or fusion to @jit for one function, or set the environment variable before importing Parakeet.

Setting Default Environment variable Meaning backend "auto" PARAKEET_BACKEND see Backends bounds_check True PARAKEET_BOUNDS_CHECK raise IndexError for bad indices fusion True PARAKEET_FUSION fuse array expressions into single loops tiling True PARAKEET_TILING tile matmul-shaped loops for cache locality (see Performance) skip_transforms () PARAKEET_SKIP_TRANSFORMS names of middle-end passes not to run ("dead code", "vertical fusion", "filter fusion", "sibling fusion", "reduction interchange", "tiling"; comma-separated in the environment) tile_bytes half of L2 PARAKEET_TILE_BYTES bytes of operand data in one tile blas True PARAKEET_BLAS hand float matrix products to the BLAS NumPy uses (CPU backends; not yet on Windows, where PARAKEET_BLAS=force opts in) num_threads all cores PARAKEET_NUM_THREADS threads used by multi-core backends parallel_grain 8192 PARAKEET_PARALLEL_GRAIN minimum iterations per chunk for cheap loops device_threshold 32768 PARAKEET_DEVICE_THRESHOLD minimum work (elements × estimated inner iterations each) for a loop to go to a GPU; the loop also needs 1024 elements (or this many, if smaller) device_reduce_chunks 8192 – partial results used by GPU reductions device_fallback "warn" PARAKEET_DEVICE_FALLBACK "warn", "silent" or "error" when a loop cannot run on the GPU cc auto PARAKEET_CC, CC C compiler executable cflags () – extra compiler flags opt_level 3 – compiler optimisation level fast_math False – allow value-changing floating-point optimisations cache_dir per-user cache PARAKEET_CACHE_DIR where compiled modules are stored print_operators False PARAKEET_PRINT_OPERATORS print the operator IR before the middle-end passes (print_indexified_function) print_ir False PARAKEET_PRINT_IR print the IR of everything compiled print_code False PARAKEET_PRINT_CODE print the generated C verify True PARAKEET_VERIFY run parakeet.verify before passes, after each pass, and after lowering (opt_verify)

PARAKEET_CUDA_SIMULATE=1 makes backend="cuda" use the CPU simulator described in Backends.

Misspelt setting names raise AttributeError listing the valid ones.

The default cache directory is ~/Library/Caches/parakeet on macOS, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/parakeet (or ~/.cache/parakeet) on Linux and %LOCALAPPDATA%\parakeet\Cache on Windows.

docs.title: Compile-time errors
docs.text:
Everything Parakeet cannot compile is reported when the function is first called with a given set of argument types, as a subclass of parakeet.CompileError:

Exception Meaning UnsupportedError a Python or NumPy feature outside the supported subset TypeInferenceError (also a TypeError) types that cannot be reconciled, wrong arguments StaticValueError (also a ValueError) something that must be a compile-time constant is not, or is invalid

The message carries the source line, a caret under the offending expression, and — because calls are inlined — the chain of calls that led there:

parakeet.errors.TypeInferenceError: indices must be a scalar, got str 'a'
  File "model.py", line 15, in helper
    return v[k] * 2
           ^^^^
called from
  File "model.py", line 21, in outer
    total += helper(x, "a")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

err.location and err.call_chain give the same information programmatically, and a note records the argument types being compiled.

docs.title: Run-time errors
docs.text:
Generated code raises ordinary exceptions, with a note pointing at the source line that failed:

@jit
def third(x):
  return x[2]


third(np.zeros(2))
# IndexError: index 2 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 2
#   raised by compiled code at demo.py:5 (in third)
Situation Exception index out of range IndexError shapes that do not broadcast, bad reshape, ragged map results, empty reduction without identity ValueError //, % or / by zero on Python numbers ZeroDivisionError assert AssertionError allocation failure MemoryError writing to a read-only array ValueError

Checks are also performed inside parallel loops and GPU kernels. When an error occurs, temporaries allocated so far are released.

NumPy array arithmetic follows NumPy: integer division by zero yields 0 and floating-point operations yield inf/nan rather than raising.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
backend="python" : Run the original function. If the answer is still wrong the bug is in your code, not in the compiler: f(x, _backend="python").

f.specialize(*args) : Compile for example arguments without running and return a Specialization: .operators (maps and reductions over index spaces, as elaborated), .ir (typed loop IR after the passes), .source (C), .kernels (GPU kernel sources), .signature.

f.inspect(*args) : Print the IR.

parakeet.config.print_ir, parakeet.config.print_code : Print the IR / C of everything as it is compiled (also PARAKEET_PRINT_IR=1).

@jit(fusion=False) : Evaluate every array expression into its own temporary. Useful to check whether a problem is related to loop fusion.

parakeet.find_broken_transform(fn, inputs) : Switch the optimizations on one at a time — fusion, each pass of the middle end (dead code, vertical fusion, filter fusion, sibling fusion, reduction interchange, tiling), the C optimizer, parallel loops, the GPU — and name the first one that makes the result differ from plain Python (or from expected, if given).

parakeet.clear_cache() : Delete cached compiled modules (they are keyed by the generated source and compiler, so this is never needed for correctness).

If you hit a parakeet.errors.InternalError or a CCompilerError, that is a bug in Parakeet: the message includes where the generated source was kept. Please open an issue with it.

docs.title: Kernel gallery
docs.text:
These examples compile ordinary NumPy functions and explicit data-parallel operators. Each code sample comes from the runnable gallery. From an installed source checkout, run the examples and their numerical checks with:

python examples/algebraic_gallery.py

The examples use import numpy as np, import parakeet and from parakeet import dsl. The same @parakeet.jit compiles both ordinary NumPy and explicit operators such as dsl.map. The name dsl.kernel is an alias for parakeet.jit. Browse the source.

docs.title: Exact nearest neighbor
docs.text:
Find the closest reference row for each query. The outer map assigns one output per query. The inner map computes distances, and argmin returns the first reference index at the minimum.

@parakeet.jit
def exact_1nn(x_query, x_ref):
  """Exact nearest-neighbor index per query row."""
  return dsl.map(
    lambda q: np.argmin(dsl.map(lambda r: np.sum((q - r) ** np.float32(2.0)), x_ref)),
    x_query,
  )

The CPU compiler fuses the score and reduction in both this form and its broadcast NumPy equivalent. At 1,024 queries by 4,096 references, each active query strip needs an 8 KiB tile and 192 bytes of row summaries. The GPU fold developed after 1.0.0 shares each score tile within a thread block and writes one winning distance and index per query and reference tile. Both source forms run on CUDA and Metal. Release and follow-up measurements.

docs.title: Gaussian kernel regression
docs.text:
Predict each query's value by weighting the reference values by distance. The maximum, weight sum and weighted output can be updated a tile at a time. This is also the reduction at the heart of softmax attention.

@parakeet.jit
def rbf_kernel_regression(x_query, x_train, y_train, neg_gamma):
  d2 = np.sum((x_query[:, None, :] - x_train[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
  s = d2 * neg_gamma
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ y_train

docs.title: Histograms and tree splits
docs.text:
Accumulate gradients and Hessians into the same bins. When their index expressions agree, the compiler can combine the two histogram traversals. Prefix sums then give the score for each possible split.

@parakeet.jit
def gbdt_best_split(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Histogram scatter-add + prefix sums + argmax gain in 8 lines (XGBoost/LightGBM core)."""
  g_hist = dsl.iscatter(nbins, bin_ids, grads)
  h_hist = dsl.iscatter(nbins, bin_ids, hess)
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_tot = g_left[nbins - 1]
  h_tot = h_left[nbins - 1]
  g_right = g_tot - g_left
  h_right = h_tot - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

docs.title: Min-plus matrix product
docs.text:
Replace multiplication with addition and addition with minimum. Each output cell takes the cheapest two-leg path through an intermediate vertex. For an m × k matrix and a k × n matrix, the result has shape m × n. The indexed reduction avoids an m × n × k temporary.

@parakeet.jit
def tropical_min_plus(a, b):
  """One min-plus matrix product: C[i,j] = min_k (A[i,k] + B[k,j])."""
  m, n = a.shape[0], b.shape[1]
  k = a.shape[1]
  return dsl.imap(
    lambda ij: dsl.ireduce(lambda r: a[ij[0], r] + b[r, ij[1]], k, combine=parakeet.minimum),
    (m, n),
  )

docs.title: Attention and linear cross-entropy
docs.text:
Both computations can normalize scores over tiles. In attention, the running state includes the weighted value vector. Cross-entropy needs the log normalizer and the target score. The backward pass can recompute the scores from the inputs.

Causal attentionLinear cross-entropy 
@parakeet.jit
def causal_flash_attention(q, k, v):
  T = q.shape[-2]
  idx = np.arange(T)
  mask = idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :]
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = np.where(mask, np.matmul(q, np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2)) * scale, np.float32(-1e9))
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return np.matmul(e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True), v)

def cut_cross_entropy(h, w, targets):
  logits = h @ w
  m = np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
  z = logits - m
  lse = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z), axis=-1))
  picked = z[np.arange(h.shape[0]), targets]
  return -np.mean(picked - lse)

For a sliding window, restrict the mask to keys within the window. When the mask and fill permit it, whole tiles can be skipped. Algebraic laws.

docs.title: Shared keys and compressed attention
docs.text:
DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention writes expanded keys and values as matrix products. When the shape makes it cheaper, the compiler reassociates these products to operate on compressed values. Grouped-query attention shares keys and values across several query heads.

Latent attentionGrouped-query attention 
@parakeet.jit
def deepseek_mla(q, c_kv, w_uk, w_uv):
  k = c_kv @ w_uk
  v = c_kv @ w_uv
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = (q @ k.T) * scale
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ v

@parakeet.jit
def gqa_attention(q, k, v):
  # q: (B, H_kv, G, T_q, D), k, v: (B, H_kv, 1, T_kv, D)
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = np.matmul(q, np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2)) * scale
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return np.matmul(e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True), v)

docs.title: Affine scans and state-space models
docs.text:
Two successive affine updates have an affine composition. A block of updates can summarize its effect on the incoming state, then blocks can combine their summaries in sequence order. The scalar filter and matrix-state recurrence below expose two uses of this rule.

Scalar IIR filterMamba-2 recurrence 
@parakeet.jit
def iir_exponential_filter(a, b):
  T = a.shape[0]
  out = np.empty_like(b)
  s = np.float32(0.0)
  for t in range(T):
    s = a[t] * s + b[t]
    out[t] = s
  return out

@parakeet.jit
def mamba2_ssd(q, k, v, a):
  T = q.shape[0]
  out = np.empty((T, v.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
  S = np.zeros((k.shape[1], v.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
  for t in range(T):
    S = a[t] * S + k[t][:, None] * v[t][None, :]
    out[t] = q[t] @ S
  return out

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Python function + argument types
        │  elaborate (parakeet/frontend/, lib/)
        ▼
 typed loop IR (parakeet/syntax/ir.py)  ──►  f.specialize(x).ir
        │  print as C (backends/c.py)        ├─► Metal kernels (backends/metal.py)
        ▼                                    └─► CUDA kernels  (backends/cuda.py)
 system C compiler ─► shared library, cached on disk ─► called through ctypes

docs.title: Specialization
docs.text: Calling a @jit function classifies its arguments — dtype, rank and layout of arrays, the types of scalars, the structure of tuples, the identity of functions — into a type key. Each distinct key gets one compiled specialization, cached per function. Values read from globals and closures are classified the same way on every call and passed as hidden arguments, so compiled code never sees stale data.

docs.title: Elaboration
docs.text:
The frontend is a staged interpreter: it walks the function's Python AST with an environment of compile-time values and emits IR only for what must happen at run time.

  • Scalars are IR expressions with a NumPy type.
  • Tuples, slices, functions, closures, dtypes exist only at compile time. Calling a function means elaborating its body in place, so by the time IR is produced there are no calls, closures or tuples left.
  • Arrays are either concrete (a buffer plus offset, shape and strides as scalar expressions — slicing is just arithmetic on those) or delayed: a function from index to element. np.tanh(x * a) + b builds a delayed array three layers deep, and no loop is emitted until something consumes it: a store, a reduction, or the return. That consumer's loop evaluates the whole expression per element. This is how fusion happens — there is no separate fusion pass.

Three questions cannot be answered in one forward pass, so elaboration is restarted with what it learned:

  1. the type of a variable modified in a loop (x = 0 then x += 0.5 — restart with x: float);
  2. whether a delayed array must be evaluated eagerly — because it would be evaluated twice, inside a loop, or after an array it reads has been modified (which would change the answer);
  3. which arguments must be compile-time constants (axis=axis), in which case the specialization is additionally keyed on that argument's value.

docs.title: The IR
docs.text:
The result is a small imperative language: typed scalar variables, flat buffers with load/store, if, counted and unbounded loops, allocation with scoped release and runtime checks. On top of it sit four operator statements, which is as much of the original's adverb tree as the middle end needs:

  • IndexMap(shape, index, body): run body for every index; the iterations are independent.
  • IndexReduce(shape, index, body, folds): fold the values body computes at every index; each Fold has its combiner as a block of IR and, when the combiner is a known associative primitive, its name. With where, only the indices at which a predicate holds count.
  • IndexFilter(n, index, body, keep): the indices at which keep holds, in order, as a new array.
  • IndexScan(n, index, body, fold, emit): a running fold; emit runs at every index with the running value.

spec.operators prints a function at this level, spec.ir after the passes. The last pass (transforms/lowering.py) replaces the operator statements by loops and by the single parallel construct — ParLoop — that runs its body for each chunk of an index range. A parallel reduction is a ParLoop that writes one partial result per chunk, combined afterwards.

Memory management is static: a buffer belongs to the loop iteration (or function) that allocated it and is released when that scope ends, unless it flows into a longer-lived variable, in which case a reference count keeps it alive. Parallel loop bodies never touch reference counts of shared buffers.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
All targets are C-like, so one emitter (backends/cfamily.py) prints expressions and statements; subclasses supply type names, math functions and failure handling.

  • The host program is always C. Each ParLoop body is outlined into a function taking a context struct (bodies with identical IR structure up to alpha-renaming share one compiled function), and launched through a function pointer supplied at call time — the thread pool, OpenMP, GCD or a plain loop — so the same compiled module serves every CPU backend.
  • For GPU backends each eligible ParLoop is additionally printed as a Metal or CUDA kernel. At run time the host code calls back into Python, which binds the buffers and dispatches the kernel; if the loop is not eligible, is too small, or the device fails, the C version runs instead.

Scalar helper functions (Python/NumPy division and modulo semantics, integer power, shifts, NaN-propagating min/max, the random number generator) exist once as C text and are included verbatim in the C, Metal and CUDA preludes, which is why the backends agree bit-for-bit on integer results.

docs.title: Calling convention
docs.text: A compiled entry point takes flat arrays of 64-bit slots: scalars, and for each array its buffer pointer, offset, shape and strides. Results come back the same way. Arrays allocated by compiled code are handed to NumPy without copying, with a finalizer that drops the native reference; views of inputs come back as NumPy views of the caller's array.

docs.title: Transforms
docs.text:
parakeet/transforms/pipeline.py lists the passes over the operator statements, in order; config.skip_transforms leaves any of them out:

  • Dead code (simplify.py). Pure IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexFilter, IndexScan and unused Alloc statements nobody reads are removed to a fixed point (the C compiler cannot remove a parallel loop).
  • Vertical fusion (fusion.py). Producer-consumer operator pairs (Map→Map including epilogues like np.tanh(a @ b + c), Scan→Map into IndexScan.emit, Map→Filter, Map→Reduce) collapse into one operator and drop the intermediate buffer.
  • Filter fusion (fusion.py). Adjacent IndexFilters collapse into a single short-circuiting filter (Filter→Filter), and a reduction over what an IndexFilter kept becomes a guarded IndexReduce with no index array (Filter→Reduce).
  • Sibling fusion (fusion.py). Adjacent IndexReduces or independent IndexMaps over the same index space share one loop.
  • Reduction interchange (tiling.py). PermuteReductions: a strided commutative+associative IndexReduce inside a stride-1 IndexMap (np.sum(X, axis=0)) is interchanged over L1-sized strips of contiguous output columns.
  • Tiling (tiling.py). An IndexMap of rank two or more whose body is a single IndexReduce plus straight-line code is run a cache-sized tile of its last dimension at a time. Inside a tile the body is instantiated for a 2×4 block of elements (syntax/clone.py copies IR blocks) and the eight reductions are fused into one with eight folds.
  • Lowering (lowering.py). Always last: operators to loops. This is where a reduction, scan or filter that may run in parallel gets its per-chunk partial results and its second pass.

One thing still rewrites the program while it is elaborated:

  • Differentiation (autodiff.py, derivatives.py). grad elaborates its function with a tape that records each array operator applied to a differentiated value — at the level of elementwise, reduce, matmul and map, where each has a one-line derivative rule — then walks the tape backwards emitting the adjoint computation with the same building blocks. Scalars are differentiated straight from their expression trees, and a view of an array is the same view of its adjoint buffer. Assignments and stores the tape cannot account for taint what they write; reaching a tainted value during the backward pass is a compile error.

docs.title: The compiled language
docs.text: Parakeet compiles a subset of Python chosen so that every value has a type known at compile time. This page describes that subset and the places where compiled code deliberately differs from running the same function in CPython.

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
Python value Inside compiled code int, float, bool 64-bit integer / double / bool, weakly typed like NumPy treats Python scalars NumPy scalars (np.float32(1), ...) scalars of exactly that dtype NumPy arrays bool, int8–int64, uint8–uint64, float32, float64; any number of dimensions, any strides tuples (also nested) compile-time structures of the above NamedTuples and plain frozen dataclasses fields can hold scalar and array leaves and are accessible by name dictionaries with fixed string keys key order is part of the structure, with lookup by literal key lists, list comprehensions arrays (there are no Python lists in compiled code) None, strings, dtypes, functions, modules compile-time constants slice, range, zip, enumerate supported as values and in loops

float16 data is widened to float32. Complex numbers, object arrays, structured dtypes, general-purpose mutable containers, sets and arbitrary class instances are not supported; passing one raises a TypeError naming the type.

Type promotion follows NumPy 2 (NEP 50) exactly: float32_array * 2.0 stays float32, int8_array + 1 stays int8, int32_array / 2 is float64.

docs.title: Statements
docs.text:
Supported: assignment (including tuple unpacking, augmented and annotated assignment, :=), if/elif/else, for over ranges, arrays, tuples, zip and enumerate, optional else on for and while, break, continue, return anywhere, nested def and lambda, assert, raise of built-in exceptions with a literal message, pass, del.

Not supported: try/except, with, classes, generators (yield), global /nonlocal, import inside a compiled function, f-strings and print. Each of these produces an UnsupportedError at the offending line.

Loop else runs on normal exhaustion, including an empty input. A break skips the corresponding else suite. Strict zip checks lengths at exhaustion. Chained scalar comparisons evaluate each reached operand once and short-circuit.

Unfiltered multi-for comprehensions over independent ranges or arrays compile as Cartesian maps. The rightmost iterator varies fastest. A scalar consumer such as sum(x * y for x in xs for y in ys) can fuse the map into its reduction. Inner iterators with observable setup and dependent domains such as for j in range(i) are outside this subset.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• Any Python function called from compiled code is inlined — helpers do not need @jit. Recursion is therefore not possible and is reported as an error.
  • Positional, keyword, default, keyword-only and *args arguments work; **kwargs does not.
  • Functions are first-class at compile time: pass them as arguments, store them in variables, close over local variables.
  • Globals and closure variables are read on every call, like in Python. If a global changes type, a new specialization is compiled.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Compiled code follows NumPy semantics for views and mutation:

@jit
def f(x):
  v = x[1:]  # a view of the caller's array
  v[0] = 0  # ... so this modifies x
  x += 1  # in place, visible to the caller
  y = x * 2  # a new array
  x[1:] = x[:-1]  # overlapping assignment behaves as if a temporary were made
  return y
  • Basic indexing (x[i, 1:-1, ::2, None, ...]), integer-array indexing and boolean masks work for reading and writing.
  • Indices are bounds-checked (IndexError); shapes are checked when broadcasting (ValueError). Use @jit(bounds_check=False) to drop index checks.
  • Returning an input returns the same object; returning a view of an input returns a NumPy view of the caller's memory.
  • Read-only arrays may be read; writing to one raises ValueError.

docs.title: Differences from CPython / NumPy
docs.text:
One static type per variable : A variable assigned an int on one path and a float on another is a float everywhere (the usual numeric promotion). A function returning 1 in one branch and 2.5 in another returns a float from both. Types that cannot be unified — say an array and None — are an error if the variable is used afterwards.

Rank is static : The number of dimensions of every array is fixed at compile time. Functions whose result rank depends on values (for example np.squeeze(x) when it cannot be known which dimensions have length 1) ask you to pass axis=.

Compile-time constants : Some arguments must be known at compile time: axis, keepdims, the length of a shape tuple, a dtype. If such a value comes straight from an argument of the compiled function, Parakeet specialises on its value automatically; otherwise it reports which expression must be constant.

Lists are arrays : [a, b, c] and [f(x) for x in xs] build arrays. sorted(x) returns an array. There is no append.

Integer arithmetic : Python ints are 64-bit and wrap on overflow (like NumPy), they are not arbitrary precision.

float16 : Operations NumPy would compute in half precision are computed in float32.

Loop variables after a loop : A variable first assigned inside a loop body keeps its last value after the loop, but if the loop never ran it is zero (CPython raises NameError).

Random numbers : np.random functions use Parakeet's own generator (see parakeet.seed); the streams differ from NumPy's.

Parallel side effects : parakeet.map, comprehensions and array expressions may evaluate their elements in parallel and in any order. Reductions with a user-defined function assume it is associative only when Parakeet can prove it (for +, *, min, max, &, |, ^); otherwise they run sequentially.

docs.title: Fixed records at the call boundary
docs.text: Named tuples preserve their field names and result type. Plain frozen dataclasses and dictionaries with fixed string keys can contain arrays or nested records. Fields and keys are part of the specialization, while array data and scalar fields remain ordinary runtime arguments. A dictionary lookup in compiled code requires a known string key. Returning these containers reconstructs their structure and keeps the usual array view semantics.

docs.title: Migrating from Parakeet 0.x
docs.text:
Parakeet 1.0 is a rewrite for Python 3.11+. The decorator and the operators keep their names, and most 0.x programs run after the usual Python 2 → 3 changes (xrange → range, / → // for integer division, print(...)).

0.x 1.0 Python 2.7, dsltools, appdirs Python 3.11+, NumPy 2, nothing else config.backend = "openmp" still works; default is "auto", which needs no OpenMP "llvm" backend removed "interp" backend "python" (runs the original function) "cuda" via PyCUDA + nvcc "cuda" via CuPy, no toolkit install; new "metal" backend f(x, _backend="c") unchanged; also @jit(backend="c") @macro still there, with a different contract: the function gets the compiler and the compile-time values of its arguments instead of syntax nodes (this is how map, reduce and the NumPy functions are defined). @typed_macro and @staged_macro are gone — arguments such as axis are specialised automatically parakeet.testing_helpers parakeet.testing (the old name still imports) config.opt_fusion, config.print_specialized_function, config.print_generated_code still accepted, as aliases of fusion, print_ir and print_code; the other opt_* flags are gone (see Configuration) parakeet.prims.add, parakeet.ndtypes.Int64, Float64, ... unchanged tuple parameters def f((a, b)) not valid Python 3; unpack in the body typed_repr(f, args), specialize(f, args), run_python_fn(f, args) unchanged (also f.specialize(*args).ir) find_broken_transform(fn, inputs, expected) unchanged in spirit: it switches fusion, tiling, the C optimizer and parallel loops on one at a time and names the first that changes the result parakeet.frontend, parakeet.syntax, parakeet.transforms, parakeet.lib the same packages, with new contents: the staged interpreter, the loop IR, and tiling / differentiation parakeet.rank, size, shape, erf, norm, ... unchanged

docs.title: Behaviour changes
docs.text:
• Result types follow NumPy 2. In 0.x bool + bool gave an integer and integer power gave a float; now both give what NumPy gives. Python scalars no longer upcast float32 arrays.
  • Bounds are checked by default. Programs that silently read out of bounds under 0.x now raise IndexError.
  • np.array(x) copies, x += 1 updates in place, views alias — as in NumPy.
  • Globals are read at call time rather than captured at first compilation.
  • parakeet.reduce is parallel only for combiners known to be associative; 0.x assumed associativity for any function.
  • imap(f, shape) passes f a tuple whenever shape is a tuple, including one-element tuples.

docs.title: Data-parallel operators
docs.text:
Most code needs none of these — NumPy expressions and comprehensions compile to the same loops. They are useful when you want to apply your own function over an array in parallel, and they can be called directly from Python without decorating anything.

import parakeet as pk
Operator Meaning pk.map(f, x, y, ..., axis=0) (alias each) f applied to corresponding slices along axis; axis=None applies it to every scalar element pk.allpairs(f, x, y, axis=0) result[i, j] = f(x[i], y[j]) pk.outer_map(f, x, y, z, ...) the n-ary generalisation of allpairs pk.reduce(f, x, ..., init=None, axis=None, map=None) fold f over all elements, or over slices along axis; with map=g and several arrays, over g(x[i], y[i], ...) pk.scan(f, x, ..., init=None, axis=0, map=None, emit=None) running fold (a generalised cumsum); emit=h gives h of each running value pk.imap(f, shape) result[idx] = f(idx) for every index of shape pk.ireduce(f, shape, init=None, combine=add) reduce f(idx) over every index pk.parfor(f, shape) call f(idx) for its side effects, in parallel pk.filter(pred, x, ..., map=None) the elements of x for which pred is true; with several arrays, map(x[i], y[i], ...) where pred(x[i], y[i], ...) holds pk.filter_reduce(f, pred, x, ..., map=None, init=None, axis=None) reduce with f over elements where pred holds (fuses into one zero-allocation guarded reduction loop when init is given) pk.scatter_add(n, idx, vals) index-directed associative scatter-add (IndexScatter) with thread-privatized parallel lowering and exact gather adjoint pk.pmap1(f, x, w), pk.pmap2(f, x, (wx, wy)) f applied to a sliding window around each element pk.grad(f, argnum=0), pk.value_and_grad(f, argnum=0) the gradient of a scalar-valued f — see Gradients pk.dsl.show_rewrite(f, *args) inspect which of Parakeet's six algebraic laws rewrote f and view before/after IR 
pk.map(lambda row: row / row.sum(), X)  # normalise rows
pk.allpairs(lambda a, b: np.sum((a - b) ** 2), X, C)  # distance matrix, no temporaries
pk.reduce(pk.maximum, X, axis=0)  # column maxima
pk.imap(lambda ij: ij[0] * 10 + ij[1], (3, 4))  # an index-defined array

pk.reduce(pk.add, x, y, map=pk.multiply)  # a dot product; no array of products is built
pk.scan(pk.add, x, y, map=lambda a, b: a - b)  # running sum of differences
pk.filter(lambda a, b: a > b, x, y, map=pk.add)  # x + y where x > y

imap, ireduce and parfor pass an integer when shape is an integer and a tuple of integers when it is a tuple.

docs.title: Functions that return arrays
docs.text:
The function given to map may return an array; the results are stacked.

pk.map(lambda row: np.cumsum(row), X)  # shape (n, m)

All results must have the same shape — this is checked at run time (ValueError).

docs.title: Parallelism and associativity
docs.text: map-like operators evaluate elements in parallel, in no particular order. reduce runs in parallel when the combining function is recognisably one of +, *, min, max, and, or, &, |, ^ (whether written as pk.add, np.add or lambda a, b: a + b), and sequentially otherwise — so a non-associative function such as lambda acc, x: acc * 0.5 + x still gives the same answer as functools.reduce. Floating-point sums are reassociated, like NumPy's own pairwise summation: expect differences in the last digits.

docs.title: Primitive functions
docs.text: pk.add, pk.subtract, pk.multiply, pk.divide, pk.minimum, pk.maximum, the comparison and logical/bitwise operators are first-class functions for use with the operators above. Outside compiled code they behave like the NumPy ufuncs of the same name.

docs.title: Structured reductions
docs.text:
dsl.fold(lift, merge, x, init) lifts each axis-0 slice of x to a nonempty tuple or named tuple of scalar fields. The pure merge(left, right) must be associative and return the same field types. Chunks may regroup adjacent values while preserving input order. The initial state is applied once, and is the result for empty input. Read any field of the result in compiled code.

For example, affine updates s -> a*s + b compose in order with merge(left, right) = (right[0]*left[0], right[0]*left[1] + right[1]). Custom folds currently support forward evaluation.

docs.title: Tiled pairwise folds
docs.text:
On CPU, a map over queries can consume an associative structured fold over references whose inputs come from a feature reduction. For example, both the gallery's nested-map 1-NN and the following NumPy expression compile to the same tiled computation:

@pk.jit
def nearest(x, y):
  return np.argmin(np.sum((x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2), axis=2), axis=1)

The compiler evaluates a bounded rectangle of scores, folds each row, and merges consecutive tile summaries in reference order. Each summary carries the global reference index, so ties and NaNs retain their first-index semantics across tiles. The same rewrite handles other pure score reductions, including a sum of absolute differences followed by argmax. The rewrite inspector reports Pairwise map and ordered tile-summary fold when it applies.

python benchmarks/gpu_showcase.py on an NVIDIA A100 (Google Colab, 12 CPU threads, float32). The same Python source runs in every column.

docs.title: Where the GPU starts to win
docs.text:
python benchmarks/crossover.py times the same kernel across sizes. On the same kind of machine (Tesla T4, 2 CPU threads, float32), after tiling and with gradients:
