The GPU wins once each element costs real arithmetic (the Julia set from the smallest size, tanh from about 100k elements) and the result is not much bigger than the work that produced it. It ties or loses when a loop mostly moves memory, because every launch pays for the copy both ways: Harris at 4096² and all-pairs at 100k rows are slower on the device than on two CPU threads. Loops below config.device_threshold (32,768 iterations) never leave the CPU, which is why the decision tree, whose parallel loops run over 32 features, is a CPU program on every backend.

The matrix product is the tiled one: on this machine it is within 2.5–3.5× of NumPy's OpenBLAS on one core.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
Where Parakeet wins. Expressions with several operations (no temporaries, one pass over memory), code that needs a Python-level loop in NumPy (Julia set, GrowCut, pairwise kernels), and anything that can use all cores.

Where it does not.

  • Dense linear algebra, when there is no BLAS to call. A product of two float matrices is handed to the BLAS NumPy itself uses, so it costs what it costs in NumPy. Parakeet's own tiled loops run everything else that has that shape (integer products, allpairs distances, products inside a parallel map or on a GPU) and are 3–10× behind a hand-tuned BLAS.
  • Single-threaded transcendental functions. NumPy ships SIMD implementations of tanh, sin, exp, ...; Parakeet's sequential backend calls the C math library one element at a time (the tanh row). With threads it is ahead again.
  • Memory-bound loops on a GPU. On this machine the 10 CPU cores usually beat the integrated GPU unless each element needs a lot of arithmetic (arc distance, convolution). Loops that mostly move memory (norm, stencils) lose, and repeatedly launching cheap kernels over a NumPy-owned array (diffusion) loses badly because the array is copied to and from the device on every launch.
  • Tiny inputs. A call into compiled code costs a few microseconds of argument marshalling; a NumPy call on a 10-element array is cheaper.

docs.title: Tiling
docs.text:
A matmul-shaped operation is a map over pairs whose element is a reduction over data picked by each member of the pair: a matrix product, allpairs distances, a tropical product. Evaluated row by row, every row of the result sweeps over all of the second operand, which stops fitting in cache long before the arrays are large. Parakeet recognises the shape — any two-dimensional map whose element function is one reduction plus straight-line code, whoever wrote it — and does two things:

  • tiles the inner dimension, so a cache-sized block of the second operand is reused for every row before moving on (config.tile_bytes, by default half of a core's L2 cache);
  • jams the reductions of a 2×4 block of elements into one loop, so each loaded value is used several times.

Neither changes what is computed, only the order. a @ b on 1024×1024 float64 (Apple M1 Max):

one core all cores untiled 190 ms 43 ms tiled 92 ms 13 ms NumPy (Accelerate) 4.5 ms

@jit(tiling=False) or config.tiling = False turns it off. The timings above are with config.blas = False; by default a float matrix product on a CPU backend calls the BLAS and takes the NumPy time.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Prefer array expressions or comprehensions over index loops when they say the same thing: they parallelise, explicit for loops do not.
  • Keep work inside one @jit function so expressions can fuse across helper calls (helpers are inlined automatically).
  • @jit(bounds_check=False) removes index checks from explicit indexing in loops once the code is known to be correct.
  • Compiled code is specialised on whether an input is C-contiguous; contiguous arrays give the C compiler unit strides to vectorise.
  • parakeet.config.fast_math = True allows the C compiler to reorder floating-point arithmetic everywhere (results may change in the last digits).

docs.title: Core ideas, history, and boundaries
docs.text:
Parakeet began at New York University as a research compiler by Alex Rubinsteyn (@iskandr), with major contributions from Eric Hielscher (@hielscher) and Nathaniel Weinman, guidance from Dennis Shasha, and advice from Russell Power — originally hosted at parakeetpython.com and described in:

  • Alex Rubinsteyn, Runtime Compilation of Array-Oriented Python Programs (PhD thesis, NYU, 2014) — type/value specialization, data-parallel adverbs, and algebraic fusion.
  • Eric Hielscher, Locality Optimization for Data Parallel Programs (PhD thesis, NYU, 2013) — tiling, register blocking, and loop interchange over adverb trees.
  • Earlier papers and talks: HotPar '12 (Parakeet: A Just-In-Time Parallel Accelerator for Python), PyData Boston '13, and PyData NYC '13 (Python on the GPU with Parakeet).

Parakeet 1.0 is a ground-up rewrite for Python 3.11+, NumPy 2, Apple Metal, NVIDIA CUDA, and reverse-mode automatic differentiation (grad), built to preserve the algebraic spirit of those theses while generalizing their operators and fixing the places where the original rules were unsound or incomplete.

docs.title: Core thesis ideas that define Parakeet
1. Specialization replaces dynamic dispatch ([R] Ch. 3 & §6.6)
docs.text:
Python has no static types, yet numerical kernels are almost always monomorphic at each call site. Parakeet uses an untyped Python function as a template and generates a native specialization for each distinct combination of argument dtypes, ranks, memory layouts (contiguous vs. strided), and tuple structure.

When an expression's type or rank depends on a runtime value (such as axis=, a tuple length, or a unit dimension 1 that governs broadcasting), Parakeet specializes on that value automatically—resolving the famous broadcasting bug noted in [R] (200×1 + 1×300) statically.

docs.title: 2. A small closed algebra of data-parallel adverbs ([R] Ch. 4)
docs.text:
Rather than implementing hundreds of bespoke C/CUDA kernels for every NumPy function, Parakeet defines NumPy operations, comprehensions, matrix products, and einsum in terms of a tiny set of data-parallel operators (adverbs):

  • IndexMap — independent element-wise / slice-wise computation over an index space
  • IndexReduce — associative or sequential folds (including multi-carry monoids such as argmin/argmax and 1-pass online logsumexp/softmax, plus guarded FilterReduce)
  • IndexScan — prefix folds with an emit stage
  • IndexFilter — stream compaction of indices matching a predicate
  • IndexScatter — index-directed associative scatter-reductions (np.bincount, parakeet.scatter_add), lowered via thread-privatized parallel bins on CPU, CUDA, and Metal

Every higher-level construct—whether written as np.tanh(x * a) + b, a list comprehension, a @ b, np.cumsum, x[x > 0], np.bincount, or parakeet.allpairs—lowers to these five operator statements (f.specialize(*args).operators).

docs.title: 3. Algebraic fusion before loop lowering ([R] Ch. 6)
docs.text:
Once a program is expressed in adverbs, optimizations become concise algebraic identities instead of fragile loop-nest analyses, backed by a single shared IndexFacts affine analysis and BufferInfo alias/cost table:

  • Vertical fusion ([R] Fig. 6.1): Map ∘ Map (including matmul epilogues like np.tanh(a @ b + c), affine transpose/slice/stencil fusion, and cost-bounded multi-consumer fusion), Map ∘ Scan into IndexScan.emit, Map → Filter, Map → Reduce, Map → Scatter, Filter ∘ Filter (short-circuiting), and Reduce ∘ Filter ⇒ FilterReduce (single zero-allocation pass).
  • Nested map flattening ([R] Fig. 6.2, CombineNestedMaps): IndexMap inside IndexMap collapses into one multi-dimensional IndexMap, exposing the full 2D/ND index space to multi-core CPUs and GPUs.
  • Horizontal / sibling & online monoidal fusion ([R] Fig. 6.3): adjacent IndexReduces (x.min(), x.max(), x.argmin(), x.argmax()) and independent IndexMaps (np.sin(x), np.cos(x)) share one loop, and dependent m = max(x); s = sum(exp(x - m)) pairs collapse into a single parallel associative (m, s) monoid pass via Fold.carries (logsumexp, 1-loop softmax).
  • Dead-operator elimination: pure maps, reductions, scans, filters, scatters, and unused allocations nobody reads are removed before lowering.

Parakeet 1.0 also adds the side conditions the original thesis omitted: single-use / cost guards (so fusion never silently duplicates expensive work), alias tracking, explicit associativity checks (non-associative folds stay sequential), and keeping SIMD-vectorizable float sums separate from non-SIMD folds.

docs.title: 4. Generalized tiling & locality from the same algebra ([H] 2013)
docs.text:
Cache, register, and GPU SRAM locality optimizations all operate on the same operator IR via two composable operators—IndexTile and TileStage—rather than recovering structure from raw for loops:

  • Reduction interchange (PermuteReductions): when an IndexMap wraps a strided commutative+associative IndexReduce whose outer map index has unit stride (np.sum(X, axis=0)), the reduction is hoisted outside an L1-sized strip of contiguous output columns.
  • Invariant map splitting & unit-axis squeezing: keepdims=True unit axes are squeezed and inner reductions independent of trailing map axes are hoisted (softmax, layer_norm), eliminating redundant $O(M \cdot N^2)$ recomputation and collapsing multi-pass row normalizations into single L1-resident loops.
  • Nested IndexTile + TileStage (CPU cache/register & GPU SRAM): any N-D IndexMap wrapping an IndexReduce plus straight-line code (a @ b, batched 3D+ matmul, allpairs, einsum, fused prologues & epilogues) is rewritten into nested IndexTile(level="cache") → IndexTile(level="register") operators on CPU (arbitrary N-D register jamming with exact remainder-face partitioning) and automatically extracts maximal row/col/k prologue TileStages into a SharedTilePlan for GPU backends.
  • GPU __shared__ (CUDA) & threadgroup (Metal) block tiling & hardware matrix units: queried via TargetProfile, analytically sized (BM, BN, BK, TM, TN) tiles (up to 64×64×32 on CUDA and 64×64×16 on Metal with bank-conflict-free padding) stage arbitrary fused prologues into SRAM once per tile and keep fused epilogues (np.tanh(a @ b + c)) in registers with zero extra HBM round-trips. On Apple Silicon Metal, float32 sum-of-products contractions automatically emit hardware simdgroup_matrix<float, 8, 8> (full IEEE FP32); on CUDA sm_80+ GPUs, config.tensor_cores=True (or fast_math=True) emits nvcuda::wmma TF32 Tensor Core kernels.
  • Persistent GPU residency (DeviceArray): parakeet.to_device(tree) and parakeet.to_host(tree) keep weights, gradients, and optimizer state tuples resident on CUDA/Metal across @jit calls with zero per-step host↔device copies.

docs.title: 5. Verifiable, inspectable, fail-loud compilation
docs.text:
• parakeet.verify (config.verify / legacy opt_verify) checks scoping, typing, and buffer-ownership invariants before passes, after every pass, and after lowering.
  • f.specialize(*args).operators, .ir, .source, and .kernels expose every stage of compilation.
  • parakeet.find_broken_transform bisects the pipeline one pass at a time.
  • Unsupported Python/NumPy constructs fail at compile time with the exact source caret and inlined call chain instead of silently falling back or returning wrong numbers.

docs.title: The boundary: what does not work yet
docs.text: Parakeet is an array-oriented numerical compiler, not a drop-in replacement for all of CPython or SciPy. Knowing the boundary up front avoids surprises:

docs.title: Python language & types
docs.text: Works Not supported yet bool, int8–int64, uint8–uint64, float32, float64 scalars & arrays (any rank/strides) Complex numbers (complex64/complex128), native float16 compute (float16 is widened to float32), structured/record dtypes, object/string arrays Nested tuples, NamedTuples, fixed string-key dictionaries, plain frozen dataclasses, slice, range, zip, enumerate Dynamic dictionary keys, set, runtime string manipulation, arbitrary user-defined classes and methods List literals and comprehensions as fixed-shape arrays Mutable/dynamically resized Python lists (.append, .extend, ragged lists) if/elif/else, for, while, break, continue, early return, nested def/lambda, closures, assert, raise try/except, with, generators (yield), global/nonlocal, import inside @jit, **kwargs, recursion Static array rank; compile-time specialization on axis, keepdims, dtype, tuple lengths Value-dependent output rank (e.g. unguided np.squeeze(x) without axis=), dynamically typed variables that cannot unify

docs.title: NumPy & SciPy library coverage
docs.text:
Roughly 200 core NumPy functions and ufuncs are built in (see Supported functions), covering arithmetic, reductions, scans, sorting, indexing/masks, @/dot/einsum, np.linalg.norm, and parallel np.random. Not yet built in:

  • Matrix decompositions and solvers (np.linalg.svd, solve, inv, eig, cholesky, qr, det, lstsq)
  • Signal/spectral transforms (np.fft.*)
  • Variable-cardinality set/grouping ops (np.unique, np.lexsort, np.isin)
  • SciPy modules (scipy.special, scipy.optimize, scipy.ndimage, ...)

docs.title: Automatic differentiation (grad / value_and_grad)
docs.text:
grad differentiates element-wise ops, reductions (sum, prod zero-safe, min, max, general folds, active initial), cumsum, sort, @ (and stacks), einsum, views/concatenation, gather/scatter, map/allpairs with user functions, and pure runtime if branches—enough to train small transformers (examples/nanogpt.py) and convnets (examples/convnet.py). Boundaries:

  • Still an elaboration-time tape, not yet an IR-to-IR pass: differentiation records operators during elaboration rather than transforming IndexMap / IndexReduce statements directly.
  • No dynamic-length loops over differentiated values: for loops with a compile-time-known length (≤ 4096, such as transformer layers or kernel offsets) unroll and differentiate; while loops or loops over runtime array lengths are refused (rewrite with reduce/map/scan).
  • Pure runtime if branches only: both branches execute and are selected by the condition, so branches touching differentiated values cannot contain array stores, return, break, or raise.
  • Missing derivative rules (refused loudly): cumprod, convolve, user-defined scan combiners, in-place indexed assignment (out[idx] = v; use parakeet.scatter_add / np.bincount(..., weights=w) for differentiable scatter-add), and overwriting an array still needed by an earlier operation's backward pass.
  • Second derivatives: work for element-wise ops, reductions, @, and views; not yet supported through map, gather indexing, or cumsum.

docs.title: GPU & locality boundaries
docs.text:
• Apple Metal has no hardware float64: float64 loops fall back to CPU cores with a warning; use float32 for Metal acceleration.
  • No per-thread heap allocation on GPU: a ParLoop that allocates temporary arrays or selects between buffer aliases inside the loop body runs on the CPU instead of CUDA/Metal.
  • GPU matrix multiplication & cuBLAS: CPU backends call BLAS for standalone float A @ B; GPU backends run Parakeet's cooperative __shared__ (CUDA) / threadgroup (Metal) block-tiled kernels — including Apple Silicon simdgroup_matrix (exact FP32, automatic) and NVIDIA nvcuda::wmma TF32 Tensor Cores (config.tensor_cores=True on sm_80+) — handling arbitrary contractions, fused prologues like sin(a) @ cos(b), allpairs, and fused epilogues like np.tanh(a @ b + c) in a single kernel, rather than calling cuBLAS. Very large standalone GEMMs are still faster in hand-tuned cuBLAS, while fused contractions and custom allpairs workloads benefit directly from single-kernel SRAM reuse.
  • Online autotuning & tiled scans: tile sizes are chosen analytically from cache/SRAM/register budgets (config.tile_bytes, GPU shared-memory budget) rather than Hielscher's runtime online search, and chunked GPU TiledScan is not yet implemented.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer and NumPy 2.
  • A C compiler: the Xcode command line tools on macOS (xcode-select --install), gcc or clang on Linux, MinGW-w64 gcc or LLVM clang on Windows.

Install the release in your Python environment. For development, run python -m pip install . in a checkout.

pip install "parakeet==1.0.0"
python -c "import parakeet; print(parakeet.available_backends())"

available_backends() reports, for every backend, either "ok" or the reason it cannot be used on this machine and how to fix that.

docs.title: Your first compiled function
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from parakeet import jit


@jit
def rms(x):
  return np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x))


x = np.random.rand(1_000_000)
rms(x)  # first call: compiles for (float64 array, 1-d), then runs
rms(x)  # later calls: straight into native code
rms(x.astype(np.float32))  # a new specialization, compiled on demand

Compilation takes a few hundred milliseconds per specialization (most of it in the C compiler) and is cached on disk, so a second run of your program starts fast.

jit also works without the decorator syntax, including on lambdas and on NumPy functions:

fast_rms = jit(lambda x: np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x)))
parakeet.run(rms.fn, x)  # compile-and-call in one step

docs.title: Loops, comprehensions, helpers
docs.text:
Anything in the supported subset can be mixed freely. Helper functions are inlined automatically — they do not need their own @jit.

def sqr_dist(a, b):
  return np.sum((a - b) ** 2)


@jit
def nearest(X, centroids):
  return np.array([np.argmin([sqr_dist(x, c) for c in centroids]) for x in X])

docs.title: Picking a backend
docs.text:
@jit(backend="metal")  # per function
def f(x): ...


f(x, _backend="c")  # per call
parakeet.config.backend = "threads"  # process-wide
with parakeet.options(backend="c", num_threads=1):  # temporarily
  f(x)

See Backends and GPUs.

docs.title: Looking inside
docs.text:
spec = rms.specialize(x)  # compile without running
print(spec.ir)  # the typed, fused loop IR
print(spec.source)  # the generated C

def rms(x_1: array[float64, 1d]):
    nchunks_9: int64? = @num_chunks(x_n0_3, True)
    partials_10 = alloc(float64, nchunks_9)
    parallel[reduce] for chunk_11, (start_12, stop_13) in chunks(x_n0_3, n=nchunks_9):
        x_15: float64 = (x_1[(x_off_2 + start_12)] * x_1[(x_off_2 + start_12)])
        acc_14: float64 = x_15
        for i_16 in range((start_12 + 1), stop_13, 1):  # simd
            x_17: float64 = (x_1[(x_off_2 + i_16)] * x_1[(x_off_2 + i_16)])
            acc_14: float64 = (acc_14 + x_17)
        partials_10[chunk_11] = acc_14
    acc_8: float64 = 0.0
    for i_18 in range(0, nchunks_9, 1):
        acc_8: float64 = (acc_8 + partials_10[i_18])
    red_19: float64 = acc_8
    res_20: float64 = sqrt((red_19 / float64(x_n0_3)))
    return res_20

No temporary for x * x exists: the multiplication was fused into the parallel reduction.

docs.title: When something is not supported
docs.text:
You get a CompileError pointing at your code, not a crash:

parakeet.errors.UnsupportedError: numpy.fft.fft is not supported in compiled code
  File "demo.py", line 6, in spectrum
    return np.fft.fft(x)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Run the function uncompiled at any time with backend="python" to tell a bug in your code from a limitation of the compiler. More in Errors and debugging.

docs.title: Release benchmarks
docs.text:
Five forward workloads compare Parakeet with general-purpose array compilers and specialist libraries. The tables report warmed median latency. Smaller values are faster. Download all timing samples and validation results (JSON).

Four CPU threads, exact 1-NN, float32. Panels show queries × references × features, with independent time scales. At the small shape Faiss took 0.033 ms. At the large shape Parakeet's NumPy function took 6.593 ms and its nested-map DSL took 6.132 ms.

On the NVIDIA A10, Faiss led large exact search and compiled PyTorch led Gaussian regression. Parakeet beat PyKeOps for both at the large shape. All GPU comparisons ran on the same physical card.

docs.title: Memory and dispatch
docs.text: The CPU IR allocates a 16 × 128 float32 score tile (8 KiB) and 192 bytes of row summaries per active query strip. The CUDA broadcast form allocates a float32 query-by-reference matrix (16 MiB at the large shape) and runs two kernels. The nested DSL form allocates one reference-length row inside the query loop. Strict CUDA execution rejected it at both sizes. On Metal we also verified the fallback diagnostic for the DSL and two launches for broadcasting. These are IR allocations and dispatch counts. Peak process memory was not measured.

docs.title: Attention, linear cross-entropy and split finding
docs.text:
All three workloads run forward on the A10. Attention has one batch, four heads, 512 tokens and head width 64. Cross-entropy includes projecting 512 vectors of width 128 to 2,048 logits and taking the mean target loss. Split finding includes two weighted histograms over 262,144 rows and 256 bins, prefix sums and the best-bin and gain return.

NVIDIA A10 implementation Causal attention Linear cross-entropy GBDT split Parakeet 0.386 1.604 0.276 PyTorch SDPA / cross_entropy / scatter_add 0.090 0.069 0.225 torch.compile over the same PyTorch functions 0.116 0.088 0.175 JAX jit 0.217 0.133 0.188 CuPy 0.326 0.255 0.420

Parakeet issued one launch and zero transfers for attention and Gaussian regression. Linear cross-entropy issued two launches and one download per call. Split finding issued six launches, two uploads and six downloads. Two clear follow-ups are a GPU schedule for ordered pairwise folds and keeping the histogram-to-split computation resident. The cross-entropy result calls for a measured choice between materializing logits and recomputing them at this shape.

docs.title: How to reproduce and interpret the numbers
docs.text:
Run from a checkout with the Modal client configured.

modal run tools/modal_release_bench.py --output comparison.json
  • The measured compiler revision was 0345559f4b2d3c59a07ce8c1a71bfb619f690063. The subsequent NumPy scalar compatibility fix concerns count_nonzero, which none of these workloads calls. The GPU reported 23,028 MiB and driver 620.70.06. The CPU reservation was four vCPUs with four library threads, and Modal hid the CPU model.
  • Inputs were generated once per provider from the same fixed seed, using float32 values and integer indices. The oracle used float64 NumPy, exact nearest-neighbor and split indices, and tolerances of rtol=5e-4, atol=3e-5 for floating outputs. SciPy's tree uses double precision internally. All published timings passed their checks.
  • GPU inputs were uploaded before timing. The comparison includes dispatch, output production, internal transfers and synchronization for every call. Faiss database insertion, tree construction, sklearn fitting, imports and initial input upload were outside query timing. This measures repeated queries against a prepared reference set.
  • Each method ran once for first-call timing and validation, then three warmups, then 21 synchronized GPU samples or 11 CPU samples. Providers ran sequentially in separate processes on the same GPU. JAX used its own Python environment. PyTorch used highest float32 matmul precision with TF32 disabled, JAX used highest precision, and Parakeet used strict device fallback, a threshold of one and tensor cores disabled. PyTorch SDPA selected its own float32 backend.
  • First-call time includes execution and any lazy compilation. The large shape follows the small shape, so first calls can reuse specializations. For causal attention, Parakeet's first call took 1.692 s and its warmed median was 0.386 ms. The raw file includes first-call times, every sample, versions, validation error and the two strict-dispatch rejections. Download the measurements.

docs.title: Rewrite rules and optimizations
docs.text:
Everything Parakeet does to a program between your source and the loops it runs, in one place, and how that compares with the two theses that describe the original system:

  • [R] Alex Rubinsteyn, Runtime Compilation of Array-Oriented Python Programs (NYU, 2014) — the operators and their fusion rules.
  • [H] Eric Hielscher, Locality Optimization for Data Parallel Programs (NYU, 2013) — tiling.

The short version: the rules are the same algebra, applied in two places.

  • While elaborating. An array expression is a delayed value — a function from index to element — and the vertical fusion rules fire at the moment an operator is applied to one. F ∘ G below means "the element function of the result is F applied to the element function of the argument"; no pass looks for the pattern afterwards.
  • In the middle end. What elaboration produces is the original's indexified level: statements IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, and IndexScatter over index spaces, with ordinary scalar code as their bodies (Specialization.operators prints it). Passes rewrite those statements — invariant-check/unit-axis normalization, dead code elimination, vertical fusion (exact and affine map/scan/filter/reduce/scatter), filter fusion (filter-filter and filter-reduce), sibling and online monoidal fusion (reductions, maps, and 1-pass logsumexp/softmax), Law 3 bilinear contraction reassociation & MLA weight absorption, Law 1 & 5 2-level monoidal tiling (flash_monoid, monoid_lse, FlashDecoding Split-K, GQA head-group folding, and affine tile-interval pruning), Law 4 chunkwise state-space duality & parallel affine prefix scan (TileScan), target-aware reduction interchange and tiling — and a last pass, LowerAdverbs in spirit, turns them into loops. parakeet.transforms.pipeline.PASSES is the list; find_broken_transform switches its members on one at a time. See Algebraic laws & frontier kernels for the mathematical laws behind these passes and Gallery of examples for runnable benchmarks.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
[R] §4.6 here Map(f, X1..Xn, axis) map(f, x1, ..., xn, axis=0), each; axis=None for every scalar OuterMap(f, X1..Xn, axis) outer_map(f, x1, ..., xn), allpairs(f, x, y) IndexMap(f, shape) imap(f, shape) Reduce(f, ⊕, X1..Xn, init, axis) reduce(⊕, x1, ..., xn, map=f, init=, axis=) IndexReduce(f, ⊕, shape) ireduce(f, shape, init=, combine=⊕) Scan(f, ⊕, emit, X1..Xn, init, axis) scan(⊕, x1, ..., xn, map=f, emit=, init=, axis=) Filter(f, pred, X1..Xn) filter(pred, x1, ..., xn, map=f) ParFor(f, bounds) parfor(f, bounds) IndexFilter(pred, shape) what x[mask], np.nonzero and filter are built on: an IndexFilter statement FilterReduce, IndexFilterReduce filter_reduce(⊕, pred, x1, ..., xn, map=, init=, axis=) — and any reduction over a filter also becomes one (see fusion) IndexScan(f, ⊕, emit, shape) what scan, np.cumsum and np.cumprod are built on: an IndexScan statement, whose emit is a block (it stores the running value) — IndexScatter (parakeet.scatter_add, np.bincount): index-directed associative scatter-add with thread-privatized parallel lowering and exact gather adjoint — grad(f), value_and_grad(f)

Every NumPy function is defined in terms of these: np.sum is a reduce, np.cumsum a scan, a @ b and np.einsum a map of reductions, a comprehension an imap.

docs.title: Vertical: a producer into its consumer
docs.text:
rule ([R] Fig. 6.1) status Map(g, Map(f, X)) ⇒ Map(g∘f, X) yes — including affine coordinate inversion (AffineInlineBufferLoad) for transpose, shifted-slice, and stencil fusion, plus cost-bounded multi-consumer fusion Map(g, IndexMap(f, σ)) ⇒ IndexMap(g∘f, σ) yes OuterMap(g, Map(f, X1), X2..) ⇒ OuterMap(λ. g(f(x1), x2..), X1..) yes Reduce(g, ⊕, Map(f, X)) ⇒ Reduce(g∘f, ⊕, X) yes Reduce(g, ⊕, IndexMap(f, σ)) ⇒ IndexReduce(g∘f, ⊕, σ) yes Scatter(⊕, idx, Map(f, X)) ⇒ IndexScatter(⊕, idx, f(X)) yes (transforms/fusion.py): elementwise weight maps fuse directly into np.bincount / parakeet.scatter_add Scan(g, ⊕, ε, Map(f, X)) ⇒ Scan(g∘f, ⊕, ε, X) yes Filter(g, pred, Map(f, X)) ⇒ Filter(g∘f, pred∘f, X) yes: the predicate and the kept values both read the unfused map Map(g, Filter(f, pred, X)) ⇒ Filter(g∘f, pred, X) yes: the selected elements are a delayed gather that the map fuses into Map(g, Scan(f, ⊕, ε, X)) ⇒ Scan(f, ⊕, g∘ε, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): a consumer IndexMap whose single input is an IndexScan's output fuses into the scan's emit block (np.cumsum(x) * 2.0 + 1.0 runs in one scan pass) Reduce(g, ⊕, Filter(f, p, X)) ⇒ FilterReduce(g∘f, ⊕, p, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): becomes a guarded IndexReduce with no index array (see below) Filter(g, p2, Filter(f, p1, X)) ⇒ Filter(g∘f, p1 ∧ (p2∘f), X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): short-circuiting single compaction, which also feeds into FilterReduce

Side conditions. [R] states one: nothing may modify the intermediate array between producer and consumer, decided by alias analysis. Here every delayed array records how many stores had happened when it was created; if a store that may alias what it reads has happened by the time it is consumed, elaboration restarts with that expression evaluated eagerly where it was written.

[R] states no condition on how often the intermediate is used, so fusing could duplicate work. Here a delayed array that costs more than a few operations per element may be consumed once; a second consumer, or a consumer inside a loop, triggers the same restart. That is the main correction to the thesis's rules.

docs.title: Nested: a map of maps
docs.text:
rule ([R] Fig. 6.2) status Map(λxi. Map(f, xi), x) ⇒ Map(f, x) yes, when the inner map is cheap and its shape does not depend on xi: the result is one delayed array over the whole index space Map(λxi. Map(f, y), x) ⇒ OuterMap(f, x, y) yes, same condition IndexMap(λi. IndexMap(f, σ2), σ1) ⇒ IndexMap(f, σ1 ++ σ2) yes, same condition

When the inner map is expensive, elaboration emits a nested IndexMap writing directly into its row of one output array (no per-row allocation), and the middle-end vertical fusion pass (CombineNestedMaps) flattens it into a single multi-dimensional IndexMap whenever the inner shape does not depend on the outer index — exposing the full 2D/ND index space to multi-core CPUs and GPUs.

docs.title: Horizontal: two consumers of one array
docs.text:
rule ([R] Fig. 6.3) status a = Reduce(f, ⊕1, X); b = Reduce(g, ⊕2, X) ⇒ a, b = Reduce(f×g, ⊕1×⊕2, X) yes, as sibling fusion (transforms/fusion.py): two IndexReduce statements over the same index space, the second not using the first's result, become one statement with two folds. x.min(), x.max() reads x once a = Map(f, X); b = Map(g, X) ⇒ a, b = Map(f×g, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): two pure IndexMap statements over the same index space where the second does not read what the first writes share one loop (np.sin(x), np.cos(x) reads x once)

Conditions the thesis leaves out: the index spaces must be provably equal (the same expression once shape variables are resolved), both seeded or both unseeded, and both must stay vectorizable — a float sum is not fused with a max, which would cost the sum its SIMD loop. Scalar definitions between the two statements are stepped over when they do not use the first result.

Tiling (below) uses the same rule on copies of one reduction.

docs.title: Filter fusion
docs.text:
rule ([R] Fig. 6.1) status Reduce(g, ⊕, Filter(f, p, X)) ⇒ FilterReduce(g ∘ f, ⊕, p, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): an IndexFilter followed by an IndexReduce over what it kept becomes one guarded IndexReduce over the filter's own index space. np.sum(x[x > 0]) is one parallel loop and allocates nothing (about 3× faster on 5M elements) Filter(q, Filter(p, X)) ⇒ Filter(p ∧ q, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): adjacent IndexFilter statements where the second filters the first's survivors collapse into one short-circuiting IndexFilter (and if reduced afterwards, into one FilterReduce) Map(f, Filter(p, X)) ⇒ one loop half: the map is a delayed array over the kept indices, so it fuses with its consumer (or directly into FilterReduce) but a returned filter still compacts first

Conditions: nothing else reads the kept indices (returning x[mask] keeps the filter); the reduction has an init, because the first element may not survive (np.min(x[mask]) stays two steps so that an empty selection still raises); it runs in parallel only when every fold has an identity to start a chunk from. If the number of survivors is used (np.mean), counting it is one more fold. Inside the fused loop the bounds check on the gathered index is dropped: the index is the loop's own.

docs.title: Reductions and scans
docs.text:
• Associativity. [R] calls the combiner "commutative" and never requires associativity; [H] requires both. Here a fold is regrouped (run in chunks, vectorized) only when its combiner is recognisably one of + * min max and or & | ^, however it was written (np.add, lambda a, b: a + b). Any other function is folded strictly left to right.
  • Several axes at once. Reduce over axes A of X ⇒ a map over the other axes of one reduction over a block: the reduced axes are moved last (a view) and each block is folded in a single pass.
  • A reduction with carried state (Carry). argmin/argmax fold (value, index) pairs per chunk and combine the pairs in index order, so the first of equal elements still wins. The same Fold.carries monoid machinery also fuses dependent m = max(x); s = sum(exp(x - m)) pairs into a single parallel associative (m, s) pass (fuse_online_logsumexp) for 1-pass logsumexp and zero-temp softmax.
  • Parallel scan. Scan(⊕, X) with an associative primitive ⇒ fold every chunk; prefix the chunk totals; scan every chunk from its prefix.
  • Parallel filter. X[mask] ⇒ count per chunk; prefix the counts; every chunk writes its survivors from its own offset.

docs.title: Linear algebra
docs.text:
• a @ b ⇒ Map((i, j) ↦ Reduce(+, a[i, :] * b[:, j])): a map of reductions like any other, so it fuses with what feeds it.
  • Layout. The inner loop should walk both operands with stride one: b is replaced by its transpose copied once, unless it is already the transpose of a contiguous array, and transpose(transpose(x)) ⇒ x.
  • Stacks. A @ B with B a matrix ⇒ reshape the stack to one tall matrix, one product, reshape back.
  • Einstein summation. einsum(spec, X1..Xn) ⇒ view every operand in one index space (output labels, then summed labels), multiply element-wise, reduce the trailing block. 'ij,jk->ik' exactly ⇒ @.
  • BLAS. A product of two float matrices outside a parallel loop ⇒ cblas_?gemm from the library NumPy itself uses, with the transpose flags set for transposed views. (config.blas = False keeps the generated loops.)

docs.title: Tiling
docs.text:
[H] here PermuteReductions: interchange a strided inner reduction with a stride-1 outer map yes (transforms/tiling.py, target-aware reduction interchange): on CPU, when an IndexMap of any rank wraps a commutative+associative IndexReduce whose inner axis is strided while the map's last index has unit stride (np.sum(X, axis=0)), the reduction is hoisted outside an L1-sized strip of contiguous output columns; on GPU (TargetProfile.is_gpu), interchange is skipped so warp/SIMD threads coalesce across columns directly Map(f, X) ⇒ TiledMap(f↑, X), applied recursively through a nest of adverbs, stopping at a Reduce generalized IndexTile + TileStage operators (syntax/ir.py, transforms/tiling.py, transforms/lowering.py): any IndexMap of rank ≥ 2 wrapping one IndexReduce (any number of folds and Carry states) plus straight-line prologues/epilogues (a @ b, batched 3D+ matmul, allpairs, einsum, np.tanh(a @ b + c)) is rewritten into nested IndexTile(level="cache") → IndexTile(level="register") operators on CPU, and extracts maximal row/col/k TileStages for GPU __shared__ (CUDA) and threadgroup (Metal) block tiling (backends/tiled_gpu.py) register tiling: a second, innermost tiling with compile-time tile sizes, then unroll and scalar-replace general N-D register jamming (lowering.jam_register_tile) on CPU (exact hyper-rectangle partition jamming 2×4 interior blocks and partial remainder faces) + 4×4 / 2×2 per-thread register micro-tiles on CUDA and Metal TiledReduce, TiledScan PermuteReductions (L1 column-strip tiled reduction) + invariant row-reduction hoisting (split_invariant_map / squeeze_unit_map for softmax and layer_norm); TiledScan not yet implemented cache tile sizes found by an online search between a pessimistic and an optimistic estimate analytical compile-time sizing from queried TargetProfile (parakeet/target.py: CPU L1/L2/SIMD, CUDA SMs/SMEM/compute capability, Metal threadgroup memory/Apple7 simdgroup_matrix), with hardware matrix-unit lowering (simdgroup_matrix on Metal, nvcuda::wmma TF32 on CUDA sm_80+ with config.tensor_cores=True) aborts unless each function body is a single adverb (simple algorithm) aborts unless the element is exactly one reduction; anything else is a plain parallel map

[H] reports that tiling slows down a stencil (an 11×11 blur). Stencils are not a map of reductions over two different operands, so they are never tiled here.

docs.title: Scalars and shapes
docs.text:
Done while expressions are built; there is no simplification pass:

  • constant folding with NumPy's semantics;
  • x + 0, x - 0, x * 1, x // 1 ⇒ x and x * 0 ⇒ 0 for integers (not floats: -0.0 and nan); select(c, a, b) with constant c; not not x; and/or with a constant side;
  • x ** 2 ⇒ x * x, x ** 0.5 ⇒ sqrt(x), x ** 1 ⇒ x;
  • a slice of a slice, a transpose, a reshape of a contiguous array, an expand_dims are arithmetic on offset and strides: no copy, no loop;
  • dimensions proven equal (by a broadcast check that already ran) are not checked again; an index known to be within its loop's bound gets no bounds check.

Specialization on values ([R] ch. 6.6 partially evaluates on inputs equal to 0 or 1). Here: a dimension of length 1 is always a constant (which is what makes broadcasting static — [R] lists 200x1 + 1x300 as giving a wrong answer); a scalar argument or an array dimension becomes a constant when the code needs one (axis=, the length of a tuple, a loop that has to be unrolled).

Left to the C compiler, which does them well on the loops it is given: common subexpressions, dead code, loop-invariant code motion, scalar replacement, unrolling, vectorization. [R]'s pipeline did these itself, on its own IR.

docs.title: Parallelism and placement
docs.text:
• Every map, reduction, scan, filter and parfor is a parallel loop over chunks; a parallel loop inside another is a sequential one.
  • A loop goes to the GPU when elements × estimated inner iterations per element reaches config.device_threshold: a short loop over long rows goes, a long loop of cheap elements below the threshold does not.
  • Between the loops of one call, arrays stay on the device. Host code that reads or writes array memory itself asks for the device's copies first.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
grad(f) adds one rule per operator, applied in reverse order of the operators f applied (details):

operator adjoint of its argument, given the adjoint ȳ of its result Map(f, X) element-wise Map(∂f/∂x · ȳ, X), summed over broadcast dimensions Reduce(+, X) ȳ broadcast to X Reduce(max, X) ȳ where X equals the result, shared between ties Reduce(*, X) ȳ · result / X, with a zero-safe branch (exact when one or more elements are zero) Reduce(f, X), any f the fold replayed backwards over its stored running values Scan(+, X) Scan(+) of ȳ from the other end A @ B ȳ @ Bᵀ and Aᵀ @ ȳ view (slice, transpose, reshape) the same view of the adjoint gather X[i] scatter-add of ȳ at i sort(X) gather by the sorting permutation, so: scatter by it Map(f, X) with any f f differentiated again per element, in parallel, each chunk adding to its own copy of the adjoints if c: A else: B both run; values and adjoints are selected by c

docs.title: What the theses have that this does not
docs.text:
• Differentiation as an IR-to-IR pass over the operator statements (here grad still records operators on a tape during elaboration, while element-wise expressions fuse both by construction during elaboration and in the middle-end vertical fusion pass).
  • Recursive tiling of deeper adverb nests, TiledReduce/TiledScan, and the online search for tile sizes.
  • Its own low-level optimizer (it relies on the C compiler instead).

docs.title: What this has that the theses do not
docs.text:
• Differentiation; einsum; products of stacks.
  • Parallel scans, filters and index-carrying reductions.
  • The cost and single-use conditions on fusion, and checked aliasing.
  • Static unit-dimension broadcasting; break/continue/early return; bounds and shape checks that raise.
  • Metal and CUDA kernels from the same loops, launch by work, arrays resident on the device.
